 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. Harrison Barnes didn't need Ja'Kobi Gillespie's 25-point game on 9 of 14 from the field and 4 of 8 from 3-point range against Utah to realize the undersized rookie guard is a talented shooter.
 "After practice, we do our little shooting games," the veteran forward said. "The first couple of days, I was like, 'He's shooting that thing a little bit.' "
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Gillespie, 22, has continued to impress. At practice Monday, he sank 12 consecutive shots from deep in a contest pitting him against Barnes, Julian Champagnie and David Jones-Garcia.
 "His confidence has continued to grow," Barnes said. "He's going to be a good player."
 Gillespie credits his sharpshooting to his father and three older brothers, all of whom helped him hone his jumper while they competed in shooting games at their home in Greeneville, Tenn.
 Who are the 2026-27 Spurs? Here is this season's roster breakdown 
 "We all kind of grew up as shooters," Gillespie said. "One of my older brothers, that's all he did, and he was probably the best shooter growing up. But I learned from all of them."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The Spurs selected Gillespie in the second round of the 2026 NBA Draft impressed by the sturdy 6-foot-1, 180-pound Tennessee alumnus' impressive stroke after he averaged 18.4 points over 37 games as a senior and shot 36.1% from long range on 5.4 attempts over four college seasons.
 His play during training camp and the preseason has reinforced that impression.
 "It's pretty consistent," Spurs guard Jordan McLaughlin, who has taken the rookie under his wing, said of his protege's shot. "He gets a lot of arc on it and has got a good spin and rotation on the ball. He's pretty strong, pretty explosive as well. He's a very good shooter."
 Gillespie is also confident, something Spurs coach Mitch Johnson pointed out when asked about the two-way contract player before last Friday's 123-97 win over Sacramento in the preseason finale.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Gillespie finished with 11 points on 3 of 4 from distance in 10 minutes to end the preseason averaging 14 points on the strength of 50% shooting from deep on 4.8 attempts per outing.
 San Antonio Spurs rookie Ja'Kobi Gillespie sings for the crowd during a rookie karaoke challenge after the Silver & Black Scrimmage at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. (Sam Owens/San Antonio Express-News)
 "He's got a really good way about him for a rookie who's a two-way," Johnson said. "Typically, that's a survival spot, (where) it's normal to be a little on edge or hard to be comfortable in your own skin. He does a really good job of having this quiet confidence and competitiveness while still being comfortable in his own skin. That's a hard balance to have in his position and I admire it for a young man that's going through this deal for the first time.
 "It's (only) been four preseason games, but I loved his aggressiveness and confidence on the court. If you're going to make mistakes, do it that way."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement McLaughlin agreed.
 BACK AT IT: Wembanyama, Spurs face Thunder in heavyweight season opener 
 "Ja'Kobi's got a lot of fight in him," the eighth-year pro said. "He's very smart, very heavy on the court, a tough defender as well. He's fit in perfectly and should be in the league for a while."
 Gillespie credits his increased comfort level to having a good grasp of the playbook and clear direction from the coaching staff.
 "It just continues to grow the more I learn what they want and just all the little concepts," he said. "It's definitely going to keep continuing to grow the more I'm in practice and just playing with the guys."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The Spurs have had success in the past with second-round picks. It's a conversation that begins, of course, with Hall of Famer Manu Ginobili (drafted in 1999). Others on the list included Patty Mills (selected by Portland in 2009), DeJuan Blair (2009), Davis Bertans (2011) and most recently Tre Jones (2020).
 "I've seen all those guys and I think it's just because of the organization," Gillespie said. "Obviously, those are good players, but the organization really takes care of you even if you're a second-round pick and gives you the resources to be good."
 San Antonio Spurs guard Ja'kobi Gillespie, center, loses control of the basketball as Utah Jazz guard Darryn Peterson, left, defendes Gillespie up the court during an NBA basketball game, Monday, Oct. 12, 2026, in Salt Lake City. (AP Photo/Tyler Tate) (Tyler Tate/Associated Press)
 The veterans have also offered plenty of help before he heads to Austin for seasoning in the G League.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I feel like all of them kind of have, but since J-Mac is at my position, I ask him a lot of questions when I want to know something or didn't hear something," Gillespie said. "(De'Aaron) Fox, Julian, a lot of the guys have helped."
 Gillespie also benefited from good coaching long before he reached the Spurs, starting with his youth coaches, Jerel Heyward and Jeremy Garner, who pushed him hard in practice.
 "I used to have football practice and then basketball practice, so I would have a long day and I wouldn't want to be there sometimes and they would get into me and make me go hard," Gillespie said. "That definitely helped me."
 "We were trying to get that pretty boy out of him," Garner told The Daily Orange, the student newspaper at Syracuse, before the Orangemen defeated the Volunteers 62-60 in December 2025. "He was a cute little kid, and we were trying to make him into a pitbull."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Playing for coach Brad Woolsey at Greeneville High, Gillespie helped the Greene Devils win consecutive state titles in 2021-22. After attracting attention primarily from mid-majors, he played his first two years of college at Belmont in Nashville before spending his junior season at Maryland.
 Under former Texas coach Rick Barnes at Tennessee, Gillespie led the Volunteers to the Elite Eight of the 2026 NCAA Tournament.
 Now, he's determined to succeed at the next level.
 "He's had a really great summer leading into camp and played well in camp," Harrison Barnes said. "It's great to see him get some more minutes (in exhibition play) and get his feet under him. Some of those first plays and possessions, he was like, 'This is moving a little fast.' It's good to see him settling in and doing his thing."
